title: De Novo Design of Miniprotein Binders Targeting the Leptin-Binding Site of the Leptin Receptor
summary: The leptin receptor (LEPR) regulates appetite, energy balance, glucose homeostasis, and neuroendocrine function and is closely associated with obesity, diabetes, and neurological disorders. Activation of LEPR signaling suppresses appetite and promotes energy expenditure, whereas impaired LEPR signaling and leptin resistance are commonly associated with obesity. Accordingly, modulation of LEPR signaling is a potential therapeutic strategy for obesity and related metabolic disorders. In this study, we report the de novo computational design of miniprotein binders targeting the leptin-binding site within the cytokine receptor homology 2 (CRH2) domain of LEPR. Computational screening and biochemical characterization identified the miniprotein binder Mini-19484, which adopted a stable α-helical fold and exhibited enhanced resistance to proteolytic degradation. Mini-19484 bound the LEPR CRH2 domain with high affinity, with a dissociation constant (Kd) of 30 nM. Structural analysis of the predicted model and mutagenesis studies revealed that Arg18 of Mini-19484 serves as a critical interaction hotspot for LEPR binding. The predicted binding mode of Mini-19484 differed substantially from that of natural leptin, providing a distinct molecular scaffold for targeting the LEPR CRH2 domain. These findings provide a valuable framework for developing miniprotein-based therapeutics targeting LEPR.

title: Sidetrak: a de novo-designed miniprotein targets the kinesin-1 coiled-coil stalk to inhibit MAP7 binding and disrupt mitochondrial transport
summary: The coiled-coil domains of cytoskeletal motors contain regulatory surfaces that offer largely unexploited targets for manipulating intracellular transport. The microtubule-associated protein MAP7 promotes kinesin-1 motor activity, binding a coiled-coil surface that overlaps the TPR docking site (TDS), a regulatory interface involved in autoinhibition. Starting from an AlphaFold3 model of this relatively feature-poor surface, we used BoltzGen to design Sidetrak, a 36-amino acid miniprotein that binds kinesin-1 with nanomolar affinity. Binding requires the TDS and is abolished by mutation of the predicted Sidetrak interface, supporting the modelled local geometry of the targeted coiled-coil region. Sidetrak inhibits MAP7 binding, reduces MAP7-dependent kinesin-1 recruitment to microtubules in cells and causes perinuclear redistribution of mitochondria, a kinesin-1 cargo. Sidetrak binds all three kinesin-1 heavy-chain paralogues, and quantitative interaction proteomics revealed selective association with endogenous kinesin-1 complexes and associated cargo adaptors. These findings demonstrate selective disruption of a motor-MAP interaction by a de novo-designed protein and highlight regulatory coiled-coil surfaces as targets for manipulating intracellular transport. Beyond providing a means to manipulate intracellular transport, this work illustrates the potential of de novo protein design to test structural models of protein interfaces and probe endogenous protein networks to uncover underlying cellular mechanisms.

title: Massively parallel quantification and prediction of monomeric protein yield in Escherichia coli
summary: Abstract  Obtaining sufficient quantities of purified proteins in their intended molecular states is essential for biological research and protein engineering. Advances in computational protein design have expanded the functional capabilities of de novo proteins and accelerated candidate generation. However, reliable methods for ranking expected monomeric yield of candidate de novo designs, including molecular binders, fluorescent proteins and enzymes, have yet to be established. Standardized measurements of monomeric yield across diverse sequences remain scarce, limiting our understanding of its determinants and the development of accurate predictors for candidate selection. Here we developed a scalable pooled assay combining peptide barcodes, size-exclusion chromatography and mass spectrometry to quantify monomeric yield for over 39,000 natural protein domain variants, de novo proteins and nanobodies under uniform and standardized Escherichia coli production conditions. We used this dataset to (1) quantify the relationship between folding stability and monomeric yield, (2) benchmark inverse-folding methods, (3) evaluate the utility of structure-prediction confidence metrics in selecting high-yield design candidates, and (4) identify sequence and structural patterns in nanobodies associated with monomeric yield and monomer-to-dimer yield ratios. We further developed ESMC-MonoYield, a protein language model fine-tuned to predict monomeric yield from amino acid sequence alone, and prospectively demonstrated enrichment of high-yield candidates among BindCraft-designed binders. Our approach enables standardized, large-scale measurement of monomeric yield across diverse proteins, and establishes monomeric yield as a sequence-encoded property that can be learned, predicted and ultimately designed.
